paragraphs.heading: What the cycle is
paragraphs.text: The oceanic carbon cycle is made of processes that exchange carbon between different pools inside the ocean, and between the ocean and the atmosphere, the seafloor and Earth's interior. It is central to the global carbon cycle. Part of it turns carbon from non-living matter into living matter and back.

paragraphs.heading: A very large store
paragraphs.text: The total active pool of carbon at Earth's surface, over spans shorter than 10,000 years, is roughly 40,000 gigatons. A gigaton is one billion tons. About 95% of that pool sits in the ocean, and most of it is dissolved inorganic carbon. In this form the oceans hold the largest pool of reactive carbon on the planet.

paragraphs.heading: The forms carbon takes
paragraphs.text: Carbon compounds are sorted two ways: organic or inorganic, and dissolved or particulate. Inorganic carbon is carbon not bound to other carbon. It is found mainly in simple compounds: carbon dioxide, carbonic acid, bicarbonate and carbonate are examples. Organic carbon is built into molecules with carbon-carbon bonds, and it forms the backbone of compounds such as proteins, lipids, carbohydrates and nucleic acids. The dissolved and particulate pools are split by a physical test: a 0.2 μm filter lets dissolved carbon through and holds particulate carbon back.

paragraphs.heading: Three pumps
paragraphs.text: Three main processes, called pumps, bring carbon dioxide from the atmosphere into the ocean interior and spread it through the oceans. They are the solubility pump, the carbonate pump and the biological pump. The solubility pump is the dissolving of atmospheric carbon dioxide into seawater, which is how dissolved inorganic carbon is introduced.

paragraphs.heading: How living things move carbon
paragraphs.text: Photosynthesis can turn dissolved inorganic carbon into particulate organic carbon, which is made up of living and dead organisms, their fecal matter and detritus. As organic carbon particles sink and are respired, dissolved inorganic carbon increases with depth. Marine life stores very little carbon, about 3 Gt, next to about 610 Gt in land vegetation. Yet the amount of carbon the two groups exchange is nearly equal, about 50 Gt each. Most particulate inorganic carbon is the CaCO₃ that makes up the shells of various marine organisms.

paragraphs.heading: The human effect
paragraphs.text: Until the Industrial Revolution, the ocean was a net source, giving CO₂ to the atmosphere. Now most of the carbon entering the ocean comes from CO₂ in the atmosphere. In recent decades the ocean has taken up around a quarter of the CO₂ that humans produce by burning fossil fuels and changing land use. In doing so it has acted as a buffer, somewhat slowing the rise of CO₂ in the atmosphere. This absorption has also made the oceans more acidic.
